Sum of squares total
Sum of squares total (SST) = Sum of squares regression (SSR) + Sum of squares error (SSE)
A simple linear regression (SLR) can be used to assess the degree to which variations in a dependent variable are explained by variations in an
independent variable. Outputs of a regression analysis include the:
sum of squares total (SST), the variation in the observed values of the dependent variable versus its average value,
sum of squares regression (SSR), the proportion of variation of the dependent variable explained by changes in the independent variable,
and
sum of squares error (SSE), the proportion of variation of the dependent variable unexplained by changes in the independent variable.
F-statistics are used to evaluate the goodness of fit (ie, how well the regression model fits the data). F-statistics reflect the explained versus
the unexplained variation in the dependent variable, adjusted for sample size and degrees of freedom (ie, mean square regression [MSR] /
mean square error [MSE]). For a given data set, both the SSR and SSE increase as sample size increases:
In this scenario, both the SST and SSE double when the sample size doubles. This indicates the same relative variance is exhibited by both
samples. Since the divisor in calculating the F-statistic is inversely related to sample size, other things equal, a larger sample size exhibiting the
same relative variation results in a greater value for the F-statistic (Choices A and B).
A larger sample size that exhibits the same relative variation of the dependent variable should give an analyst greater confidence regarding the
explanatory power of the independent variable.

explanation_en:
A contingency table is used to display the frequency distribution for multiple categorical variables simultaneously. Each row displays a
unique variable outcome of the first categorical variable, and each column displays a unique variable outcome of the second categorical variable.
The contingency table shows:
the marginal frequency of each categorical variable, which is the total frequency for each row or column.
the joint frequency of two categorical variables, which is the frequency in each cell.
The observed values are from a sample (ie, subset of a population) and are not representative of the whole target population. The population's
expected joint frequency of the two specified categorical variable outcomes is the product of the individual relative marginal frequency of each
categorical variable outcome, in this case, growth stock and large-cap stock:

question_en: An analyst studies the relationship between company size and bond rating to predict bond defaults. The following table represents the number of defaults over a 10-year period: Based on this information, the relative frequency of BBB–BB bond defaults by mid-cap companies, based on all mid-cap company bonds, is closest to:
explanation_en:
Contingency table
Company size
Rating Large cap Mid cap Small cap Total by rating
AAA or A 15 32 51 98
BBB or BB 24 47 68 139
High yield 31 55 70 156
Total by size 70 134 189 393
Contingency tables can be used to find patterns that exist between two variables. Each variable can have one or more categories; the only
requirement is that the number of categories be finite. One variable (eg, company size) is placed in rows and the other (eg, bond rating) is placed
in columns. Each cell in a contingency table represents a joint frequency between a category of one variable and a category of the other variable.
Data in a contingency table can be displayed as a count (ie, absolute frequency) or a percentage of a total (ie, relative frequency).
In this question, the variables are bond rating and company size, and each variable has three categories. There are 47 defaults of bonds rated
either BBB or BB from mid-cap companies and 134 total bond defaults from mid-cap companies, so the relative frequency is 47 / 134 ≈ 35.1%.
When using contingency tables, it is crucial to know precisely which relationships are being compared. For instance, if this question had asked for
the frequency of BBB- or BB-rated mid-cap defaults relative to all defaults of BBB—BB bonds, the correct answer would be 47 / 139 ≈ 33.8%
(Choice C). If the question had asked for the frequency of mid-cap defaults with those ratings relative to all defaults, the correct answer would be
47 / 393 ≈ 12.0% (Choice A).

question_en: The following data is for a firm operating under perfect competition: If the price per unit is €5, economic profits are maximized when the firm produces:
explanation_en:
Under perfect competition, firms face a horizontal demand curve with the market price equal to marginal revenue. The level of output that
maximizes economic profit is also the economic breakeven, where marginal revenue (MR) equals marginal cost (MC) and average total cost
(ATC): MR = MC = ATC. At that point, production of:
additional units would result in an economic loss, wherein MR < MC and ATC, and
fewer units would result in a missed profit, wherein MR > MC.
In this case, profit is maximized at 105 units, the point at which MR per unit (ie, €5 market price), MC, and ATC are all equal.

option_a: The firm can expect to earn zero economic profit.
option_b: Zero economic profit means that the firm generated an accounting loss.
option_c: The firm should produce goods at a level at which marginal revenue exceeds average total
explanation_en:
Economic profit is the difference between a firm's total revenue, which is price (P) × quantity sold (Q ), and its total cost, which is cost (C) ×
E

Any firm in a perfectly competitive industry should always produce the quantity of goods at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost. In the
short run, a firm can earn an economic profit; this is reflected in the yellow rectangle shown above. However, since there are no barriers to entry
in perfect competition, additional sellers are attracted by the potential economic profit and enter the industry.
The increased supply from these new entrants causes the market price to fall to the point where marginal revenue, marginal cost, and average

question_en: The following table lists various economic indicators and the trend in each one over the past several months for an economy. This mix of economic indicators most likely forecasts near-term future economic:
explanation_en:
Certain economic and financial measures have historically exhibited consistent patterns indicating the stage of the business cycle. These
economic indicators are characterized as leading, coincident, or lagging indicators.
Leading indicators provide the most value to investment practitioners since they signal changes in real GDP several months to a year in
advance. Coincident indicators move largely in tandem with the economy, and lagging indicators trail changes in the economy by several months
or quarters. How specific indicators are classified will vary from country to country, but leading indicators that are consistent across most
economies include:
Interest rate spread
Residential building permits/construction
Stock market performance
New manufacturing/machinery orders
Business confidence/expectations
In this scenario, all three leading indicators are indicating a period of economic deceleration or slowing growth in the coming quarters.
Residential building permits and new orders for manufacturing have been in steady decline. The interest rate spread is the difference
between short-term rates and long-term rates. A narrowing of the spread, as is the case here (ie, the yield curve flattened by 1%), implies
economic deceleration.

question_en: In an economy that operates under an exchange rate targeting policy, which of the following conditions is most likely?
option_a: The central bank is required to maintain a fixed policy interest rate.
option_b: Monetary policy can focus on internal rather than external considerations.
option_c: Target country inflation (deflation) is imported regardless of the effect on the domestic
explanation_en: Monetary policy targets Stated Long-run Country policy target economic goal characteristics Fixed rate or Price stability leading to better long- Inflation range for specified run performance price index Larger, Optimize across more developed economies Interest multiple goals Target adjusted over business cycle rates (employment, GDP growth) Smaller, Exchange Fixed rate or range versus target Stability versus economies of major less developed rate currency trading partners with significant import/export sectors The goal of monetary policy is to optimize economic welfare, although central banks are given a variety of policy targets intended to attain that goal. Central banks may have: One policy target (ie, single mandate) that guides all policy actions: A specific inflation target (eg, 2%) or a specified range An exchange rate target, which is a fixed level or band of values versus a major currency (eg, EUR) Multiple policy targets that seek an optimal balance among potentially conflicting goals: High employment GDP growth Stable prices Stable exchange rate When a country uses exchange rate targeting, its policies are designed to maintain an exchange rate target (or range) with another currency, usually from a larger and/or more stable economy. As a result, if the target currency's economy experiences inflation or deflation, so does the economy that targets it. In this situation, since all policy actions must be aimed at maintaining the targeted currency exchange value, the targeting economy gives up monetary policy independence. This may adversely affect both the targeting economy and its ability to address any adverse effects. For example, exchange rate targeting may keep a central bank from exercising independent monetary policies based solely on domestic conditions, such as maintaining a fixed policy interest rate or adjusting monetary policy (Choices A and B).

question_en: Which of the following trade policies is most appropriate for a country to enact if it is trying to reduce a large trade deficit?
option_a: Reduce import tariffs on raw materials and manufactured goods by an average of 50%.
option_b: Impose import quotas limiting foreigners to 20% of a domestic market in which imports constitute 5% of the market.
option_c: Negotiate a voluntary export restraint agreement with a country running a large trade surplus
explanation_en: Quotas, tariffs, and voluntary export restraints are the policies most commonly used to reduce trade deficits. Imposing quotas or levying tariffs on imports directly impacts commercial counterparties. Alternatively, agreements with foreign governments are used to restrain their firms from exporting to the domestic market. Although the specific mechanisms of each policy differ, all restrict foreign sales in the domestic market. All else constant, the trade balance is favorably affected as reduced imports shrink trade deficits or increase trade surpluses. Voluntary export restraints are negotiated with countries currently running large surpluses. Foreign governments agreeing to constrain their exports will reduce domestic imports. Effective voluntary export restraint agreements reduce trade deficits. (Choice A) Reducing tariffs on raw materials and manufactured goods tends to make those foreign-sourced items less expensive. Tariff cuts increase imports, which leads to higher trade deficits. (Choice B) Import quotas normally reduce trade deficits. Limiting foreign producers to a 20% market share in a market where foreign sales account for only 5% of sales is an ineffective way to reduce the trade deficit.

question_en: An analyst has compiled the following information: Country Z is an open economy, trading at world prices, and does not currently trade with any of the other three countries. Assuming equal consumption of both commodities, which country will benefit the most from a trading relationship with Country Z?
explanation_en: An autarky is a country that produces all goods and services consumed internally and does not trade with others. An autarkic economy is considered a closed economy. Domestic prices within a country are a function of its ability to produce those goods with only domestic resources and are known as the autarkic prices. Countries that do not place restrictions on imports and exports are known as open economies. Open economies are said to practice free trade as they import and export at the world's price for goods and services (eg, Country Z). The further away the world price is relative to a country's autarkic price, the greater the potential trade benefit for the autarky. A country's terms of trade benefit the most if world export prices are greater than its autarkic price and world import prices are less than its autarkic price since the country can achieve greater purchasing power. In this scenario, all the autarkies produce coffee below world price and sugar above world price. Thus, if all three traded with other countries, each would export coffee and import sugar. The net terms-of-trade improvement would be greatest for Country A since it would sell (ie, export) coffee at the world price of $1.10 and buy (ie, import) sugar at the world price of $0.40, netting a $0.50 improvement. (Choices B and C) The net terms-of-trade improvement for Country B is $0.15. For Country C, it is $0.40.

explanation_en: A tariff is one type of trade restraint. It is a tax on imported goods that is usually paid as a higher price for the goods and usually results in a loss to the net welfare of the economy. Tariffs cause inefficiencies in both the supply and production functions of the economy; these losses are known as deadweight losses. In the diagram above, the supply deadweight loss is Region B and the demand deadweight loss is Region D. Before the tariff, all suppliers had per-unit production costs of €200 or less. The tariff caused the price to increase to €250 so domestic suppliers whose production costs were greater than €200 could now compete. However, domestic supply increased (from 4 million to 6.5 million) while domestic demand decreased (from 8.2 million to 7 million), therefore the additional domestic supply represented a reallocation of resources to phones when those resources could have been better employed elsewhere in the economy, creating an inefficiency. The demand deadweight loss is evidenced from the reduced domestic demand after the tariff. Consumers who might have spent more than €200 for a phone but would not spend €250 were excluded from the market. explanation_en: Most economists believe greater overall welfare is attained when countries engage in international trade rather than by attempting self-sufficiency in meeting domestic demand (ie, autarky). The gains from international trade derive from each country concentrating on the production of goods it produces relatively more efficiently and trading for goods it produces relatively less efficiently. Gains result from specialization and economies of scale. The gains from trade are not shared equally; there are winners and losers. On one hand, industries expanding to meet export opportunities will benefit from higher prices, due to increased foreign demand, and their employees will benefit from greater job opportunities and higher wages (Choice C). On the other hand, the industries' domestic customers must pay higher prices. In addition, industries facing import competition will suffer domestic market share decline. As such industries contract, they will employ fewer workers. (Choice A) Increased trade results in greater consumer choice. This is due both to imported goods competing with domestic suppliers and the introduction of previously unavailable products.
